grammar.explanation: This pattern follows a verb's connective form and expresses completing an action or doing it unintentionally. Here it can also emphasize acting impulsively.
This pattern expresses regret about an action already taken: the speaker wishes they had not done it.
This pattern follows a dictionary-form verb and expresses a deliberate decision to do something.
This pattern follows a verb's connective form and means trying an action to see what happens.
This pattern expresses an uncertain possibility, equivalent to 'may' or 'might.' The dialogue uses its polite negative ending.
This pattern adds another requirement or fact, meaning 'not only ... but also ...'.
This pattern makes a forceful rhetorical question expressing rejection: 'Would I ever ...!' or 'Of course I would not ...!'
After a complete plain-form statement, this pattern reports information heard from someone else, meaning 'I hear that' or 'apparently.'
This pattern follows a verb and expresses an intended outcome. With a negative verb, it means doing something so that an unwanted event does not happen.
This pattern means doing something excessively or being too much of a quality. Here it means speaking too fast.
This pattern presents an action as something done for someone else. In the narrator's speech it can sound rough or condescending.
This pattern marks a time limit or endpoint, meaning until or up to.
This pattern describes a resulting state left by an intentional action. Here writing remains visible on the blackboard.
This pattern expresses completion and often regret about the result. Here the narrator regrets having come to this place.
This pattern expresses a deliberate decision to do something.
This pattern expresses contempt or criticism toward someone acting contrary to what their status supposedly permits.
This pattern forms an emphatic rhetorical rejection, meaning that something could never happen or is absurd.
This pattern links two actions performed at the same time by the same subject.
This pattern means doing something exactly as described, instructed, or demonstrated.
This pattern expresses a confident inference, meaning must be or there is no doubt.
This pattern expresses possibility or uncertainty, meaning might or perhaps.
This pattern expresses necessity or obligation, meaning must do something.
This pattern says that an action has only just happened, emphasizing how recent it feels to the speaker.
This pattern expresses emphatic refusal or denial through a rhetorical question: there is no way the speaker would do it.
This pattern means there is no choice but to perform the action.
This pattern expresses an uncertain possibility, meaning may or might. The ending can take a polite form.
This pattern expresses prohibition or something that must not be done. The ending can take a polite form.
This pattern expresses a deliberate decision to do something. Here the past form reports decisions already made.
This pattern describes having experienced an action at least once before, without specifying when it happened.
This pattern is a regional sentence ending that adds a courteous, conversational emphasis. It helps characterize the old woman's local speech.
Added to a verb stem or adjective stem, this pattern means doing something too much or being excessively a certain way.
After a clause, this pattern lists a reason or fact while suggesting there are other reasons or facts as well.
Added to a verb stem, this pattern describes an action as difficult to do.
Added to a verb stem, this pattern means easy to do or prone to happen.
With a negative verb, this pattern means taking care or making an effort to prevent something. Here it appears as a firm command.
This pattern literally says that a negative situation would be unacceptable. Here it introduces a precaution in case money runs short.
This pattern means even if or even when. Combined with a question word, it means no matter what, who, or where.
This pattern expresses an inference or information learned indirectly, meaning apparently or seems to be. It can also take a connective ending.
Attached to a verb stem, this pattern indicates two actions performed at the same time by the same person.
Following a noun, this pattern identifies the role or capacity in which someone acts.
Following a plain verb, this pattern describes an arrangement or outcome that comes about, often through circumstances or an outside decision.
